title: Spanish 3
description: Free Spanish 3 study guide: preterite vs. imperfect, future and conditional, present perfect, commands, the subjunctive, por vs. para, culture of the Spanish-speaking world and reading/listening strategies. 80 practice questions with explanations, 48 flashcards and a practice exam.

units.name: Advanced Preterite vs Imperfect

concepts.intro: The preterite presents past actions as completed, with a clear beginning or end.
b: Single completed actions: Ayer compré un libro (Yesterday I bought a book)
Actions with a specific time frame or number of times: Viví en México dos años
A sequence of events: Me levanté, me duché y salí
An action that interrupts another: Estaba leyendo cuando sonó el teléfono
Trigger words: ayer, anoche, el año pasado, de repente, una vez

concepts.intro: The imperfect describes ongoing, habitual or background situations in the past.
b: Habitual actions: De niño, jugaba al fútbol todos los días (I used to play)
Background description: Hacía sol y los pájaros cantaban
Time, age and ongoing states: Eran las tres. Tenía diez años
Actions in progress: Mientras yo cocinaba, él limpiaba
Trigger words: siempre, a menudo, todos los días, mientras, de niño

concepts.intro: Some verbs mean something different in the preterite.
b: Conocer: conocí = I met (for the first time); conocía = I knew
Saber: supe = I found out; sabía = I knew
Querer: quise = I tried; no quise = I refused; quería = I wanted
Poder: pude = I managed to; no pude = I failed to; podía = I was able to
Tener: tuve = I got/received; tenía = I had

keyFacts: Preterite = completed actions; imperfect = ongoing or habitual background.
Interrupted action: imperfect (in progress) + preterite (interruption).
Time and age in the past use the imperfect: Eran las dos; tenía doce años.
Conocí = I met; supe = I found out.
traps: 'Used to' is always imperfect, never preterite.
Duration alone doesn't force the imperfect: 'Viví allí cinco años' (a closed period) is preterite.
Don't translate 'was/were' automatically as imperfect of estar; ask whether the action was completed.

units.name: Future & Conditional

concepts.intro: The future tense adds endings to the whole infinitive.
b: Endings for all verbs: -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, -án (hablaré, comerás, vivirá)
Irregular stems: tener → tendr-, salir → saldr-, venir → vendr-, poner → pondr-, poder → podr-, saber → sabr-, hacer → har-, decir → dir-, querer → querr-, haber → habr-
Ir a + infinitive is also common for near future: Voy a estudiar
Future of probability: ¿Dónde estará Ana? (I wonder where Ana is)
Hay → habrá (there will be)

concepts.intro: The conditional expresses what would happen.
b: Endings on the infinitive: -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, -ían (hablaría, comerías)
It uses the same irregular stems as the future: tendría, haría, diría, podría
Polite requests: ¿Podría ayudarme? (Could you help me?)
Future in the past: Dijo que vendría (He said he would come)
Probability in the past: Serían las diez (It was probably ten)

concepts.intro: Conditional sentences pair specific tenses.
b: Real/likely: Si + present, future: Si estudio, aprobaré
Hypothetical: Si + imperfect subjunctive, conditional: Si tuviera dinero, viajaría
The si clause can come first or second: Viajaría si tuviera dinero
Never use the future or conditional directly after si meaning 'if'
Deber in the conditional gives advice: Deberías dormir más

keyFacts: Future endings: -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, -án on the infinitive.
Conditional endings: -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, -ían.
Future and conditional share irregular stems (tendr-, har-, dir-…).
Si + imperfect subjunctive → conditional.
traps: Don't say 'Si tendría dinero'. It should be 'Si tuviera dinero'.
Hacer → haré (not haceré); decir → diré (not deciré).
The conditional endings look like -er/-ir imperfect endings but attach to the infinitive.

units.name: Present Perfect

concepts.intro: The present perfect uses haber plus a past participle.
b: Haber: he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, han
Regular participles: -ar → -ado (hablado); -er/-ir → -ido (comido, vivido)
Irregular participles: abrir → abierto, decir → dicho, escribir → escrito, hacer → hecho, morir → muerto, poner → puesto, romper → roto, ver → visto, volver → vuelto, cubrir → cubierto
Nothing goes between haber and the participle; pronouns go before haber: Lo he visto
Participles with haber never change for gender or number: Ellas han llegado

concepts.intro: The present perfect links past actions to the present.
b: Actions in a time period that isn't finished: Este año he leído cinco libros
Life experiences: ¿Has viajado a Perú?
Recent actions with present relevance: Ya he terminado la tarea
Common words: ya (already), todavía no / aún no (not yet), alguna vez (ever), nunca
Usage varies by region: Spain uses it more for today's events; much of Latin America prefers the preterite

concepts.intro: Participles can also describe nouns.
b: With estar, the participle describes a resulting state: La puerta está abierta
As adjectives, participles agree in gender and number: las ventanas cerradas
Compare: He cerrado las ventanas (action) vs. Las ventanas están cerradas (state)
The pluperfect uses the imperfect of haber: había comido (I had eaten)
Acabar de + infinitive means 'to have just': Acabo de comer

keyFacts: Present perfect = haber (he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, han) + participle.
Irregular participles: abierto, dicho, escrito, hecho, muerto, puesto, roto, visto, vuelto.
Participles don't agree after haber; they agree as adjectives.
Acabar de + infinitive = to have just done.
traps: Don't put pronouns between haber and the participle: 'Lo he hecho', not 'He lo hecho'.
Hecho, not 'hacido'; visto, not 'veído'.
'Han llegadas' is wrong; after haber the participle is invariable.

units.name: Commands Review & Advanced

concepts.intro: Informal commands have different affirmative and negative forms.
b: Affirmative tú = él/ella present form: Habla, Come, Escribe
Irregular affirmative tú: di, haz, ve, pon, sal, sé, ten, ven
Negative tú = present subjunctive tú form: No hables, No comas, No salgas
Pronouns attach to affirmative commands (Dímelo) and go before negative ones (No me lo digas)
Add an accent when attaching pronouns to keep the stress: Cómpralo

concepts.intro: Usted, ustedes and nosotros commands come from the subjunctive.
b: Usted/ustedes: Hable(n), Coma(n), Escriba(n); negative just adds no
Irregular: vaya(n), sea(n), esté(n), dé/den, sepa(n)
Nosotros (let's): Hablemos, Comamos; ir → Vamos (affirmative), No vayamos (negative)
Reflexive nosotros drops the -s before nos: Sentémonos, Levantémonos
Spelling changes: -car → -que (busque), -gar → -gue (llegue), -zar → -ce (empiece)

concepts.intro: Commands can sound abrupt; Spanish has softer options.
b: Use usted with strangers, elders and in formal settings
Add por favor or use the conditional: ¿Podría pasarme la sal?
Vosotros commands (used in Spain): hablad, comed; the negative uses the subjunctive: no habléis
Infinitives are used for written instructions: No fumar
Double object pronouns: le/les become se before lo/la: Dáselo

keyFacts: Affirmative tú = third-person singular present.
Irregular tú: di, haz, ve, pon, sal, sé, ten, ven.
Negative and formal commands use the subjunctive.
Pronouns attach to affirmative commands, precede negative ones.
traps: Negative tú isn't just 'no' + affirmative: 'No habla' is wrong; it's 'No hables'.
Ve (go) and ve (see) look the same; context decides.
Le/les + lo/la becomes se lo/se la, never 'le lo'.

units.name: Subjunctive Deep Dive

concepts.intro: Start from the yo form of the present, drop -o, and add 'opposite' endings.
b: -ar verbs take -e endings: hable, hables, hable, hablemos, habléis, hablen
-er/-ir verbs take -a endings: coma, comas…; viva, vivas…
Yo-form irregulars carry over: tener → tenga, hacer → haga, conocer → conozca
Irregulars (DISHES): dar (dé), ir (vaya), ser (sea), haber (haya), estar (esté), saber (sepa)
Stem changes follow the present pattern; -ir stem-changers also change in nosotros/vosotros: durmamos, pidamos

concepts.intro: The subjunctive appears in a dependent clause after certain triggers, usually with a change of subject.
b: Wishes: Quiero que vengas
Emotions: Me alegra que estés aquí
Impersonal expressions: Es importante que estudies
Recommendations: Te recomiendo que duermas más
Doubt/denial and Ojalá: Dudo que llueva; No creo que sea verdad; Ojalá que ganemos

concepts.l: Other Uses and the Imperfect Subjunctive
concepts.intro: The subjunctive also follows certain conjunctions and unknown antecedents.
b: Conjunctions that always take it: para que, antes de que, sin que, a menos que, con tal de que
Cuando, hasta que, en cuanto take the subjunctive for future actions: Cuando llegues, llámame
Unknown or nonexistent antecedents: Busco un libro que explique esto
Imperfect subjunctive: ellos preterite, drop -ron, add -ra endings: hablaran → hablara, tuviera, fuera
Sequence of tenses: a past trigger takes the imperfect subjunctive: Quería que vinieras

keyFacts: Present subjunctive: yo form minus -o + opposite vowel endings.
DISHES irregulars: dé, vaya, sea, haya, esté, sepa.
WEIRDO: wishes, emotions, impersonal expressions, recommendations, doubt, ojalá.
Creer/pensar affirmative take the indicative; negative take the subjunctive.
traps: Same subject, no que: 'Quiero ir' (not 'Quiero que yo vaya').
'Creo que es verdad' (indicative) vs. 'No creo que sea verdad' (subjunctive).
Cuando with a past or habitual action takes the indicative: 'Cuando llegué, comí'.

units.name: Por vs Para & Prepositions

concepts.intro: Para points toward a goal, destination or deadline.
b: Purpose (in order to): Estudio para aprender
Destination: Salimos para Madrid
Recipient: Este regalo es para ti
Deadline: La tarea es para el lunes
Opinion and comparison: Para mí, es fácil; Para un niño, lee muy bien

concepts.intro: Por looks at cause, means, exchange or movement through.
b: Cause or reason (because of): Llegué tarde por el tráfico
Exchange or price: Pagué diez dólares por el libro; Gracias por todo
Duration: Estudié por dos horas
Means of communication or transportation: por teléfono, por avión
Movement through or along: Caminamos por el parque; also 'per': 60 millas por hora

concepts.intro: Some prepositions don't translate one-to-one.
b: Fixed expressions with por: por fin, por ejemplo, por eso, por favor, por supuesto
Verbs with a preposition: soñar con, pensar en, depender de, enamorarse de, casarse con
Prepositional pronouns: para mí, para ti, con él; con + mí/ti → conmigo, contigo
A personal: use 'a' before a specific person as a direct object: Veo a mi abuela
De + el → del; a + el → al

keyFacts: Para: purpose, destination, recipient, deadline, opinion.
Por: cause, exchange, duration, means, through.
Conmigo, contigo (not 'con mí').
Personal a before a person as direct object.
traps: Gracias por, not 'gracias para'.
'Para' + infinitive = in order to; don't use 'por' for purpose.
Pensar en = to think about; pensar de = opinion of.

units.name: Culture: Spanish-Speaking World

concepts.intro: Spanish is an official language in 20 countries plus Puerto Rico, and is widely spoken beyond them.
b: Spanish is an official language of 20 countries plus Puerto Rico (a U.S. territory), and has about 500 million native speakers
Regions: Spain, Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean, South America and Equatorial Guinea in Africa
Vocabulary varies by region: 'bus' can be autobús, camión (Mexico), guagua (Caribbean, Canary Islands) or colectivo (Argentina)
Voseo: in Argentina, Uruguay and parts of Central America, vos replaces tú (vos tenés)
The U.S. has one of the largest Spanish-speaking populations in the world

concepts.intro: The Spanish-speaking world blends Indigenous, European and African heritage.
b: Great Indigenous civilizations included the Maya, Aztec (Mexica) and Inca
Spanish colonization began after 1492; most Latin American countries won independence in the early 1800s
Many Indigenous languages remain widely spoken, such as Quechua, Guaraní (co-official in Paraguay) and Nahuatl
Spain has co-official regional languages: Catalan, Galician and Basque
African heritage shapes Caribbean and coastal music, food and culture

concepts.intro: Traditions and artists from the Spanish-speaking world are known worldwide.
b: Día de los Muertos (Mexico, Nov. 1–2) honors deceased loved ones with ofrendas
Writers: Miguel de Cervantes (Don Quijote), Gabriel García Márquez and Pablo Neruda (Nobel Prizes), Gabriela Mistral (first Latin American Nobel in Literature, 1945)
Artists: Frida Kahlo, Diego Rivera, Pablo Picasso, Salvador Dalí
Music and dance: flamenco (Spain), tango (Argentina), salsa, cumbia, reggaetón
La quinceañera celebrates a girl's 15th birthday in many Latin American communities

keyFacts: Spanish is official in 20 countries plus Puerto Rico.
Voseo (vos) is used in Argentina, Uruguay and parts of Central America.
Guaraní is co-official in Paraguay.
Gabriela Mistral: first Latin American Nobel laureate in Literature (1945).
traps: Día de los Muertos isn't 'Mexican Halloween'. It honors the dead with family remembrance.
Brazil speaks Portuguese, not Spanish.
Vocabulary differences are normal, not mistakes: 'coche' vs. 'carro' vs. 'auto'.

units.name: Reading & Listening Strategies

concepts.intro: Preparing your brain for a text makes comprehension much easier.
b: Predict content from titles, images and headings
Activate vocabulary you already know about the topic
Identify the text type (news article, ad, interview, story) and its likely purpose
Read the questions first on a test so you know what to listen or look for
Set a purpose: gist (main idea) or specific details

concepts.intro: You don't need to know every word to understand a text.
b: Cognates look similar in English and Spanish: información, importante, universidad
False cognates (falsos amigos): embarazada = pregnant, librería = bookstore, éxito = success, carpeta = folder
Use context clues from surrounding sentences
Recognize word families and parts: -mente = -ly (rápidamente); -dad = -ty (ciudad)
Skip words that aren't essential to the main idea

concepts.intro: Listening in real time requires different strategies than reading.
b: Listen for key words, numbers, names and time expressions
Pay attention to tone, emphasis and connectors (pero, sin embargo, por eso, además)
On a first listen get the gist; on a second, catch details
Native speakers link words together; practice with authentic audio (podcasts, news, songs)
Take quick notes with abbreviations rather than full sentences

keyFacts: Cognates: similar words in both languages.
False cognates: embarazada (pregnant), librería (bookstore), éxito (success).
-mente = -ly; -dad = -ty.
First listen: gist; second listen: details.
traps: 'Estoy embarazada' means 'I'm pregnant', not 'embarrassed' (avergonzado/a).
Trying to translate every word slows comprehension.
Connectors like 'sin embargo' signal contrast. Don't skip them.

quiz.q: De niña, mi hermana ___ al parque todos los domingos.
quiz.e: A habitual past action ('used to go') uses the imperfect.

quiz.q: Ayer yo ___ a las siete de la mañana.
quiz.e: A single completed action at a specific time uses the preterite.

quiz.q: Mientras nosotros ___ la cena, llegaron los invitados.
quiz.e: The action in progress (background) is imperfect; the interruption is preterite.

quiz.q: ___ las once de la noche cuando terminé la tarea.
quiz.e: Telling time in the past uses the imperfect.

quiz.q: What does 'Conocí a mi mejor amigo en 2019' mean?
o: I knew my best friend in 2019
I will meet my best friend
I met my best friend in 2019
I used to know my best friend
quiz.e: Conocer in the preterite means to meet for the first time.

o: I used to know the truth
I found out the truth yesterday
quiz.e: Saber in the preterite means to find out.
Age and life stage in the past are description: imperfect.

quiz.q: Ellos ___ en Chile por tres años y luego se mudaron.
quiz.e: A closed, completed period of time uses the preterite.

o: I didn't want to go (ongoing feeling)
quiz.e: Querer in the negative preterite means refused.

quiz.q: Hacía frío y ___ mucho cuando salimos.
quiz.e: Weather as background description uses the imperfect.
Salir has the irregular future stem saldr-.
Hacer → har- in the future.

quiz.q: Yo en tu lugar, ___ (hablar) con la profesora.
quiz.e: 'In your place, I would talk': conditional.

quiz.q: Si ___ (tener) más tiempo, aprendería a tocar la guitarra.
quiz.e: Hypothetical si clause takes the imperfect subjunctive.

quiz.q: Si llueve mañana, nosotros ___ en casa.
quiz.e: A real/likely condition: si + present → future.

quiz.q: '¿Podría decirme la hora?' is best described as:
o: A polite request using the conditional
quiz.e: The conditional softens requests.

quiz.q: Ella dijo que ___ (venir) a la fiesta.
quiz.e: Reported future in the past uses the conditional.

o: Where will my phone be tomorrow
I wonder where my phone is
quiz.e: The future can express probability or wondering in the present.
Decir → dir-.
Deber + infinitive; the conditional deberías gives advice.
Ver has the irregular participle visto; nosotros uses hemos.
Escribir → escrito; tú → has.
An irregular participle.

quiz.q: Where does the pronoun go? 'I have done it.'
quiz.e: Object pronouns go before the conjugated haber.
Volver → vuelto, invariable after haber.
As an adjective with estar, the participle agrees with tienda.
Acabar de + infinitive = to have just.

quiz.q: Which sentence uses the present perfect for a life experience?
quiz.e: Alguna vez signals experience up to now.
An action before another past action uses the pluperfect.
'Not yet' connects to the present: present perfect.
An irregular tú command.
The negative tú uses the present subjunctive.
Pronouns attach to affirmative commands, with an accent.
Pronouns go before negative commands.
Irregular subjunctive stem.
The final -s drops before nos.
-car verbs change to -que in the subjunctive.
Le becomes se before lo.
Ir uses vamos in the affirmative nosotros command.

quiz.q: Which is the most polite way to ask a stranger to repeat something?
quiz.e: Conditional + usted + por favor is very polite.

quiz.q: Quiero que tú ___ (venir) a mi fiesta.
quiz.e: A wish with a different subject triggers the subjunctive.
Impersonal expressions of necessity take the subjunctive.
Doubt triggers the subjunctive; saber → sepa.
Affirmative creer expresses belief, so it takes the indicative.
Negated belief expresses doubt: subjunctive.
Same subject: use the infinitive.
Cuando referring to a future action takes the subjunctive.

quiz.q: Busco un apartamento que ___ (tener) tres cuartos.
quiz.e: An unknown antecedent takes the subjunctive.

quiz.q: Mis padres querían que yo ___ (estudiar) medicina.
quiz.e: A past trigger requires the imperfect subjunctive.

quiz.q: Te doy el dinero para que ___ (comprar) el libro.
quiz.e: Para que always takes the subjunctive.
Recipient: para.
Thanks in exchange for something: por.
Purpose (in order to): para.
Cause/reason: por.
Movement along/through: por.
Deadline: para.
Con + mí becomes conmigo.
Exchange/price: por.

quiz.q: Anoche soñé ___ mi viaje a España.
quiz.e: Soñar con = to dream about.
The personal a precedes people as direct objects.

quiz.q: Which South American country's main language is NOT Spanish?
quiz.e: Brazil's official language is Portuguese.

quiz.q: In Argentina, 'vos tenés' is used instead of:
quiz.e: This is voseo, common in the Río de la Plata region.

quiz.q: Día de los Muertos is primarily a celebration to:
o: Honor and remember deceased loved ones
quiz.e: Families build ofrendas with photos, food and marigolds.

quiz.q: Which Indigenous language is co-official in Paraguay?
quiz.e: Most Paraguayans speak Guaraní.

quiz.q: Which language is co-official with Spanish in a region of Spain?
quiz.e: Catalan, Galician and Basque are co-official in their regions.
Published in two parts (1605, 1615).

o: Argentina and Uruguay (Río de la Plata)
quiz.e: It developed in Buenos Aires and Montevideo.

quiz.q: Frida Kahlo was a painter from:
quiz.e: Known for self-portraits and Mexican imagery.

quiz.q: Which African country has Spanish as an official language?
quiz.e: A former Spanish colony.
It marks a coming of age in many Latin American communities.

quiz.q: Which word is a true cognate?
quiz.e: Universidad means university; the others are false cognates.
A library is una biblioteca.
An exit is una salida.

quiz.q: The suffix '-mente' usually corresponds to English:
quiz.e: Rápidamente = quickly.
It introduces an opposing idea.

quiz.q: Before listening to an audio passage on a test, you should:
o: Read the questions to know what to listen for
quiz.e: Previewing questions focuses attention.

quiz.q: If you don't know a word that isn't essential to the main idea, you should:
o: Reread the whole text from the start
quiz.e: Most texts can be understood without every word.
Carpet is alfombra.

quiz.q: Predicting content from a title and images before reading is called:
quiz.e: It activates relevant vocabulary.

quiz.q: On a first listen to a passage, you should mainly focus on:
quiz.e: Details come on the second listen.

flashcards.d: Completed past actions with a defined beginning or end.
Ongoing, habitual or descriptive past (was -ing, used to).
Imperfect for what was happening + preterite for the interruption.
I met vs. I knew.
I found out vs. I knew.
I managed to vs. I failed to.
Infinitive + -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, -án.
Infinitive + -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, -ían ('would').
tendr-, saldr-, vendr-, pondr-, podr-, sabr-, har-, dir-, querr-, habr-.
¿Qué hora será? = I wonder what time it is.
Si + present → future.
Si + imperfect subjunctive → conditional.
haber (present) + past participle: he hablado.
-ar → -ado; -er/-ir → -ido.
abierto, dicho, escrito, hecho, muerto, puesto, roto, visto, vuelto.
haber (imperfect) + participle: había comido = I had eaten.
Agrees in gender/number: las puertas abiertas.
Acabar de + infinitive = to have just done something.
Él/ella present form: habla, come, escribe.
di, haz, ve, pon, sal, sé, ten, ven.
No + present subjunctive: no hables.
Present subjunctive: hable, coma, vaya.
Let's: hablemos; reflexive drops -s: sentémonos.
Attached to affirmative, before negative commands.
Yo form − o + opposite endings (-ar → e; -er/-ir → a).
dar (dé), ir (vaya), ser (sea), haber (haya), estar (esté), saber (sepa).
Wishes, emotions, impersonal expressions, recommendations, doubt/denial, ojalá.
Subjunctive needs a new subject after que; same subject uses the infinitive.
Ellos preterite − ron + -ra endings: hablara, fuera, tuviera.
para que, antes de que, sin que, a menos que, con tal de que.
Purpose, destination, recipient, deadline, opinion/comparison.
Cause, exchange, duration, means, movement through, 'per'.
por fin, por ejemplo, por eso, por favor, por supuesto.
With me / with you (informal).
Used before a specific person who is a direct object.
soñar con, pensar en, depender de, casarse con.
Use of vos instead of tú (Argentina, Uruguay, parts of Central America).

Altar with photos, food, candles and marigolds for the deceased.

PART_A.q: Cuando yo ___ (ser) pequeño, mi familia ___ (vivir) en Texas.
PART_A.e: Background description and ongoing past states: imperfect.

PART_A.q: Si ganara la lotería, ___ (comprar) una casa en la playa.
Negative tú command of 'poner': '___ los pies en la mesa.'
PART_A.e: Negative tú uses the subjunctive: pongas.

PART_A.q: Mis padres esperan que yo ___ (sacar) buenas notas.
PART_A.e: Hope/wish with a new subject: subjunctive; -car → -que.

PART_A.q: Salgo ___ Bogotá mañana y estaré allí ___ dos semanas.
Which strategy helps most on the first listen of an audio passage?
o: Focus on the gist and key words

PART_B1.q: 'Ayer supe que mi primo se casa.' Supe means:
PART_B1.e: Saber in the preterite = found out.

PART_B1.q: Ella dijo que ___ (hacer) la tarea más tarde.

PART_B1.e: Irregular participle as an adjective, agreeing with ventana.

PART_B1.q: Te llamo ___ teléfono ___ confirmar la cita.

PART_B1.e: Guagua is Caribbean and Canary Islands usage.

PART_B1.q: 'Sin embargo' in a reading passage signals the author will:

PART_B2.q: Write 4–5 sentences in Spanish about a memorable trip, using both the preterite and imperfect correctly. Underline one example of each.
PART_B2.sa: Model: Cuando tenía doce años, mi familia fue a Puerto Rico. Hacía mucho calor y el mar era muy azul. Un día visitamos El Yunque y vimos una cascada. Mientras caminábamos, empezó a llover. ¡Fue un viaje increíble! (Imperfect: tenía, hacía, era, caminábamos, for background and ongoing actions; preterite: fue, visitamos, vimos, empezó, for completed events and the interruption.)

PART_B2.q: Give advice to a new student using three different subjunctive triggers.
PART_B2.sa: Model: Te recomiendo que hables con tus profesores. Es importante que hagas la tarea todos los días. Ojalá que encuentres buenos amigos pronto. Each sentence has a trigger (recommendation, impersonal expression, ojalá), a change of subject and a correctly formed present subjunctive.

PART_C.q: Escribe un párrafo (6–8 oraciones): ¿Qué harías si pudieras vivir un año en cualquier país hispanohablante? Usa el condicional, el imperfecto del subjuntivo y el futuro.
PART_C.sa: A strong answer uses si + imperfect subjunctive → conditional ('Si pudiera vivir un año en otro país, viviría en Argentina'), the conditional to describe plans ('Aprendería a bailar tango; comería empanadas'), a real future statement ('Algún día viajaré allí'), and a cultural detail such as voseo, tango or Buenos Aires. Verb forms are accurate and it uses transitions like además and por eso.

PART_C.q: Compare two traditions or cultural products from different Spanish-speaking countries. Explain what each reveals about its culture.
PART_C.sa: A strong answer names two specific traditions (e.g. Día de los Muertos in Mexico and flamenco in Spain) with accurate details, and explains what each shows: remembrance and family ties with a blend of Indigenous and Catholic traditions for Día de los Muertos; Andalusian, Romani, Moorish and Jewish influences in flamenco. It draws a clear comparison and avoids stereotypes.
